Q1-title.text: Q1 · Where does a rule live on the thing's page?

Q1-why.text:
Q1. Where does a rule live on the thing's page?

Recommended: A, a Rules section under the lifecycle. A rule is part of a thing, like its machine, so it is a section; it adds no page kind and no tree rows, and ⌘K can still find it.

Q2-title.text: Q2 · How does a refusal say which rule refused it, in the portal, the docs, the scaffold and MCP?

Q2-why.text:
Q2. How does a refusal say which rule refused it, in the portal, the docs, the scaffold and MCP?

Recommended: A, one generated sentence. It comes from the declaration, so it reads the same on all four surfaces and can't drift; a written description can be added later where a generated one reads badly.

Q3-title.text: Q3 · Does the lifecycle mark the states a rule holds in?

Q3-why.text:
Q3. Does the lifecycle mark the states a rule holds in?

Recommended: A, no mark. The refusal already sits on the arrow that can break the rule, and the Rules section names the states in words; a badge says the same thing again in a harder code.

Q4-title.text: Q4 · Does the operation's spine get a stop for rules?

Q4-why.text:
Q4. Does the operation's spine get a stop for rules?

Recommended: A, a rules stop between the move and the commit. The spine is the runtime's own order and the rule is now a stop in it; marking the commit instead blames the store for a refusal it never made.
